title: Anthropic’s Matt Samuels and Den Delimarsky - Claude & MCP: Building the USB-C for the Legal Tech Stack
author: Matt Samuels · Den Delimarsky

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source frames tool-enabled AI as delegated, componentised work governed by firm-specific operating rules and acknowledges possible staffing effects on juniors. It does not assess whether automation will erode apprenticeship or verification expertise, nor does it advocate the cluster’s proposed reconstruction of training.
qs: So think of the tasks you normally do as a lawyer and how you delegate things to associates or junior partners.
Plus, we have these discussions about how this work is going to impact the workflow in terms of staffing, both for juniors and for adjacent professionals.

st.t: Continuous learning: Filtering matters more than release chasing
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s practical, experimentation-led approach to continuous learning and reinforces the case against release chasing by stressing that specific forecasts quickly become unreliable. It materially extends the proposition by arguing that experimentation must preserve lawyers’ strategic judgment and professional craft rather than encourage excessive delegation.
qs: The best way to take advantage of this is to use the tools and try to figure out how to apply them to your life.

But I’ll say two things that I think about in a semi-worrying way are the loss of the art and the craft of being a lawyer, people delegating too much to these tools and losing the forest for the trees, or not paying attention to the why and the strategic calls.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s human-led, selective-deployment model and materially extends it with a concrete operating architecture: MCP connections and plugins can integrate enterprise data, tools, firm-specific practices and automated checks, while administrators apply granular permissions, risk-calibrated rollout, training and human review. Its warning that over-delegation can erode strategic judgment reinforces the need to preserve lawyer responsibility and craft.
qs: But I think the next tier of evolution in the workflow goes back to what we talked about earlier, because the power of MCP is composability.
I’m optimistic people will use these more for the low-leverage tasks and focus on the strategy and the craft.

st.t: AI procurement: Product expansion exceeds realized value
st.an: The source supports shifting attention from product announcements toward workflow integration and the human consequences of deployment. It frames MCP as a possible response to fragmented legal systems and warns that excessive AI delegation could undermine strategic judgment and legal craft, while offering no demonstrated adoption or value outcomes.
qs: Marlene, for years we’ve talked about the integration tax, which is that massive headache that law firms face trying to get all of our different vertical software systems to actually talk to each other.

But I’ll say two things that I think about in a semi-worrying way are the loss of the art and the craft of being a lawyer, people delegating too much to these tools and losing the forest for the trees, or not paying attention to the why and the strategic calls.

st.t: Organisational adaptation: AI benefits require human control
st.an: Samuels supports the cluster’s core proposition that AI’s benefits depend on preserving human judgment and strategic control. He is optimistic about delegating lower-value tasks but warns that excessive delegation could erode legal craft and compromise; these are hypothetical concerns rather than empirical findings. The MCP community discussion is largely incidental to the cluster.
qs: But I’ll say two things that I think about in a semi-worrying way are the loss of the art and the craft of being a lawyer, people delegating too much to these tools and losing the forest for the trees, or not paying attention to the why and the strategic calls.
I’m optimistic people will use these more for the low-leverage tasks and focus on the strategy and the craft.

st.t: Vendor market: Expanding maps require disciplined selection
st.an: Shaver supports the cluster’s market-awareness and intermediary role by presenting curated demonstrations as a way for buyers to track new products and features. The excerpt is promotional and does not substantively address disciplined procurement, implementation, adoption or outcomes.
qs: At these new LTH events, which are free to attend, by the way, you can log in virtually to see 12 curated providers offer demos of their products.
It’s an easy way to get up to date on what’s new in the market, whether that is brand-new products or existing ones with new features.

kp.k: MCP standardizes AI access to siloed enterprise data
kp.d: Delimarsky describes Model Context Protocol as an open-source interoperability protocol addressing the gap between models’ training data and confidential organizational information. Standardized connections are intended to reduce bespoke integration work across document management, communications, databases and other applications. This is a technical explanation and claimed benefit, not a measured finding about implementation costs.
qs: It essentially creates a universal set of rails that says, if you want to use data with AI models, here’s how to do it.
It’s a massive gateway for enabling data access to any model in a way that doesn’t force people to constantly rewrite custom bespoke solutions just to access a specific data source.

kp.k: Composable connections enable cross-system legal workflows
kp.d: Delimarsky explains that multiple MCP servers can connect one AI client to different sources, allowing a lawyer to request correlations between communications and case documents without managing underlying data formats. Organizations can use official servers or build custom servers for in-house systems; the protocol does not prescribe the underlying storage or application. The Slack–iManage workflow is illustrative rather than a reported deployment.
qs: You’re not just seeing one data source, but you can go into, for example, Claude, and if you connect several MCP servers, say Slack and iManage, you can ask the LLM, you know what, I’m reviewing a case for X, Y, and Z scenario. Can you get me all the conversations that happened and then correlate them with data in iManage?
Because the SDK is open source, because it’s an open protocol, anybody can write an MCP server.

kp.k: Enterprise controls should distinguish drafting from consequential actions
kp.d: Samuels recommends tool-level permissions, role-based access control, least privilege and employee training. His email example distinguishes drafting from sending, allowing administrators to constrain actions requiring human review. He describes Anthropic’s point-and-click controls as supporting always, never or sometimes allowing tools; these are client-level controls rather than guarantees inherent in MCP.
qs: You can have it draft an email. Then, if you’re the CISO, you might not want it to send the email without a human reviewing it.
They might have draft email and send email as two different tools.
So it comes down to the admin setting rules and using standard concepts like RBAC and least privilege issues.

kp.k: OAuth connects AI access to existing user permissions
kp.d: Asked by Lambert about OAuth 2.1 and document permissions, Delimarsky explains OAuth authentication, user tokens and additional tool scopes as the mechanism for restricting access. He emphasizes that authentication does not automatically authorize every tool or dataset, and that many security conventions sit outside MCP itself. Gebauer connects this account to ethical walls and need-to-know requirements; the transcript does not present a security test.
qs: You can use OAuth to gate access to your MCP server the same way you would gate access to any website or API or any other resource.
MCP does not dictate how you do 2FA.
Then you get conversations back that only Marlene can access.
Some tools require additional scopes and say, no, before you can access this tool, you need this additional permission.

kp.k: Server approval and auditability support organizational governance
kp.d: Samuels recommends administrative approval of new MCP servers and risk-sensitive decisions about custom servers, user groups and testing periods. He identifies conversational tool-call records and a compliance API as ways to inspect activity, while describing some audit behavior in qualified terms and predicting more granular permissions over time.
qs: The admin should say, hey, I need to approve any net-new MCP server the organization wants to use.
They effectively have a dashboard where they can toggle on and off whether the server can be used at all.
The model should tell you in the conversation itself when it called the tool and what it did with it.
Then afterward, you could look at the chat and see what happened, and you can use things like the compliance API to do it at scale.

kp.k: Adoption enthusiasm rests on reported deployments and personal experience
kp.d: Gebauer reports accounts of Rio Tinto’s legal team connecting an LLM to 4.5 million iManage documents via MCP in a few days; this is the host’s framing, not a deployment finding substantiated by the guests. Samuels declines to speak for law firms but says adoption is faster than he expected before joining Anthropic. His claimed gains in triage and internal legal service derive from personal Cowork use, without quantified productivity evidence.
qs: We’ve seen reports of Rio Tinto’s legal team connecting an LLM to 4.5 million iManage documents via MCP in a few days.
I can’t speak for the law firms.
I think the speed here is faster than I would have expected before joining Anthropic.
The amount better I am at my job, and the amount I am able to triage issues and give my internal clients good legal service using that tool, is amazing.

kp.k: Agent harnesses orchestrate actions beyond document retrieval
kp.d: Delimarsky distinguishes MCP’s connecting infrastructure from the agent harness responsible for planning and executing work. Tools, resources and asynchronous tasks allow agents to retrieve documents, combine information and continue other work while remote processing completes. Samuels analogizes this to delegating component tasks to associates; the analogy does not establish staffing reductions or replacement.
qs: Ultimately, the agent harness is the one responsible for doing things with MCPs or MCP servers.
It also has primitives such as tasks, which is basically asynchronous processing.

So MCP is becoming the plumbing for a lot of these agentic harnesses where, by themselves, they can trigger actions, think through requirements that need to be done, break them down into a set of tasks, and then execute those tasks.
So think of the tasks you normally do as a lawyer and how you delegate things to associates or junior partners.

kp.k: Interactive apps could preserve familiar legal review interfaces
kp.d: Samuels illustrates how MCP apps could display deposition pages and document-review interfaces inside Claude, supporting conversational retrieval, highlighting and updates to the source of record. His deposition-provider and Relativity examples are conditional on vendors building suitable apps. The envisioned privilege-review workflow retains the human reviewer rather than asserting autonomous privilege determinations.
qs: You can ask a question that ill-formed, and if the deposition transcript company made an MCP app that’s well done, it would literally find the relevant text and populate the page.
Then I think what’s cool about MCP apps is you can theoretically highlight it or do other transformations, and it will ping back to the actual source of record and update it.
If they made an MCP app, you could start doing your doc review in Claude.
And Claude will know how to find that document, surface it to you, and then you can do the privilege review on that.

kp.k: Shared workspaces could reduce context switching and manual transcription
kp.d: Delimarsky argues that combining interactive apps with multiple MCP servers reduces copying, tab switching and separate searches across email, Slack and documents. He also describes creating Google Docs and updating notes through connected tools. Samuels says bidirectional system-of-record updates should be possible but flags latency, timing and editing conflicts; he treats Harvey’s possible MCP support as tentative.
qs: So context-switch reduction is a huge benefit right away.

You can also have another MCP server that starts a new Google Doc and says, can you put all the notes we’re working on there, summarize them as we go, so I have that one point of reference to go back to?
I think it can update the system-of-record document, but you have to be thoughtful about timing.
With Harvey itself, as they use the APIs of a lot of these LLMs, they themselves are an AI client, so they might have MCP support too.

kp.k: Skills codify firm procedures rather than replace connections
kp.d: Samuels describes skills encoding NDA rules, escalation conditions, firm voice and drafting preferences. Delimarsky distinguishes these procedural instructions from MCP connections: skills can specify which tools to use, output formatting, documentation steps and scripts for legacy applications. He claims explicit routing can accelerate work and save tokens, without providing measurements.
qs: You can package the rules around when you deviate from an NDA, when something needs to get escalated to a particular person.
People often confuse skills and MCPs and say one replaces the other. Really, as Matt said, they complement each other.
Within a skill, you can refer to MCP servers, write custom scripts, call applications that run on your machine.
So it speeds up your process and helps you save a little on tokens too.

kp.k: Plugins package procedural knowledge with executable capabilities
kp.d: Samuels describes plugins, introduced for Claude Code and then Cowork, as bundles of skills and MCP connections that can also include webhooks or subagents. His hypothetical NDA plugin combines contract-platform connections, firm voice and a signing-authority check. He also imagines evidence discoveries automatically updating litigation timelines and proof outlines; these are workflow possibilities, not documented outcomes.
qs: There’s a kind of abstraction of those called plugins that we created first for Claude Code and now for Cowork.
It might connect to Ironclad or DocuSign or whatever MCP servers you might have over there, but then it has the skills with your firm voice and you can also do other things.
An example of one of those might be, check this against, check to make sure the user of this plugin has the right authority to sign or something like that.
What if you found this golden document and it automatically added it to the timeline and added it to your proof outline?

kp.k: Knowledge management must serve agents and preserve authoritative records
kp.d: Samuels recommends that firms define systems of record and use skills to update case channels or timelines as new information is generated. Delimarsky anticipates knowledge management expanding from human access to agent usability, warning about proprietary formats and emphasizing taxonomy, organization and predictable discovery. He does not recommend one particular file format.
qs: What does a system of record look like for what we’re doing?
Now the question is, is this also helpful to agents?
Whatever format I’m storing the data in, will an agent be able to successfully access it and act on that data to provide me a summary, insights, or recap?
You still have to optimize for discovery and organization and having some kind of predictability.

kp.k: Experimentation is recommended amid explicit forecasting uncertainty
kp.d: Delimarsky recommends practical use of current tools for document review, research and connected-data workflows rather than relying on impressions of earlier models. In the closing forecast discussion, he explicitly declines to predict future developments given changes over the last six months; Samuels agrees with that uncertainty. Their recommendation is practitioner advice, not a controlled comparison of adoption strategies.
qs: Try it for reviewing documents, for doing deep research, for connecting to your data sources and applications through different MCP servers, and see what output you get.
Having seen the last six months, I have no answer for what the crystal ball holds.
Anything I say right now is going to be completely wrong in three months, six months, or a year.

kp.k: Overdelegation could erode legal judgment and professional craft
kp.d: Samuels worries that excessive delegation could weaken lawyers’ attention to purpose, strategy and professional relationships. He hopes tools will free lawyers for strategic work but imagines opposing parties repeatedly requesting maximal AI-generated redlines without meaningful compromise. This is an expressly speculative professional-risk scenario, not evidence of observed deskilling or negotiation failure.
qs: The loss of the art and the craft of being a lawyer, people delegating too much to these tools and losing the forest for the trees, or not paying attention to the why and the strategic calls.
I’m optimistic people will use these more for the low-leverage tasks and focus on the strategy and the craft.
Then the other side does that, and you are never actually compromising and thinking about what matters.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Delimarsky says MCP reduces bespoke integration work and enables AI to combine information across enterprise systems.
pts.d: At 04:28–09:34, Delimarsky describes an open protocol through which compatible AI clients can access different data sources without repeatedly building client-specific integrations. His legal-work example combines Slack conversations with iManage documents. Official or internally developed MCP servers can expose existing tools and data stores.

pts.k: Delimarsky and Samuels describe permission-controlled access and administrative oversight rather than unrestricted AI access to firm data.
pts.d: At 11:37–21:00, Samuels describes role-based access, least privilege, server approval, tool-level permissions and compliance APIs. Delimarsky explains how OAuth credentials and scopes allow servers to return only information accessible to the authenticated user. These are descriptions of security mechanisms and configured behavior, not reported security-test results or guarantees against every disclosure risk.

pts.k: Samuels reports substantial personal productivity gains and expects lawyers to benefit from connecting AI to their enterprise information.
pts.d: At 22:43, Samuels says adoption is faster than he expected and attributes the utility of Cowork largely to MCP-enabled access to Slack, Gmail and other context. He reports better issue triage and service to internal clients, but expressly declines to speak for law firms generally.

pts.k: Delimarsky says MCP provides the tools through which agents can execute multi-step work, while the agent harness supplies orchestration.
pts.d: At 26:03, Delimarsky distinguishes MCP's data-access and action primitives from the agent harness that plans and executes tasks. He describes agents combining documents and database records, initiating asynchronous searches and continuing other work. At 29:37, Samuels suggests lawyers conceptualize this through tasks they already delegate to associates, rather than making an explicit staffing-replacement prediction.

pts.k: Samuels and Delimarsky say interactive MCP apps can reduce context switching and bring legal review, retrieval and record updates into a shared AI workspace.
pts.d: At 31:55–37:47, Samuels offers conditional examples of displaying deposition pages, highlighting material and reviewing documents through a Relativity app inside Claude. Delimarsky describes combining the displayed material with email and Slack context and maintaining notes automatically. Samuels says updates should work bidirectionally but flags latency and editing-conflict considerations. The Relativity example is hypothetical, not a claim of an implemented deployment.

pts.k: Samuels and Delimarsky say skills and plugins can encode firm procedures and coordinate repeatable legal workflows.
pts.d: At 39:20–43:04, Samuels describes skills containing NDA rules, escalation instructions and firm voice. Delimarsky says skills complement MCP by specifying which tools to use and how to format and store results; he also describes instructions for legacy applications. He claims this reduces model deliberation, speeds processes and saves some tokens. Samuels describes plugins bundling these components and imagines automatically adding useful litigation documents to timelines and proof outlines.

pts.k: Delimarsky predicts that knowledge management must accommodate agents, increasing the importance of accessible formats and organized data.
pts.d: At 46:20–48:29, Samuels says organizations must rethink systems of record and can use skills to update case channels or timelines. Delimarsky predicts a shift from organizing knowledge solely for humans to making it accessible and actionable for agents. He contrasts restrictive proprietary formats with more open formats and says predictable organization improves discovery.

pts.k: Samuels anticipates possible erosion of legal craft through overdelegation, while hoping automation frees lawyers for strategy.
pts.d: At 52:37, Samuels frames this as a concern and a possible future, not an observed finding. His example is opposing parties repeatedly asking AI for maximal contract redlines rather than deciding what matters and compromising. His reference to low-leverage tasks concerns task value, not associate-to-partner staffing leverage.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source primarily offers practitioner experience, technical explanations and illustrative workflows, not quantitative evaluations.
pts.d: Samuels speaks as Anthropic's senior product counsel and a Cowork user; Delimarsky speaks as technical staff and an MCP maintainer. Samuels's productivity claims rely on personal experience and examples seen by his team. Delimarsky cites informal observations of experimentation and data-format obstacles. No measured productivity gains, legal accuracy benchmarks, security audits or adoption dataset are supplied. The Rio Tinto figure is introduced by a host and is not independently substantiated or adopted as a specific factual claim by the interviewees.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Most benefits are presented as available now with appropriate integrations and governance; future developments are explicitly uncertain.
pts.d: In the transcript labeled 2026, the speakers describe current MCP, skills and Cowork capabilities, with recent acceleration over weeks or months. Benefits depend on available or custom-built servers, capable apps and harnesses, permissions, training, usable data and attention to synchronization. Some legal workflows remain conditional illustrations. Samuels qualifies his adoption assessment by saying he cannot speak for law firms. Neither interviewee offers a firm market-transformation deadline; both disclaim confidence in forecasting.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims concern law-firm lawyers, in-house legal teams, security and operations personnel, and software providers.
pts.d: Partners and associates are described as delegating component tasks and conducting document or privilege review in integrated workspaces. Litigators may move evidence more efficiently into case artifacts; transactional lawyers may apply standardized NDA procedures but risk unproductive automated bargaining. Samuels's internal clients are the beneficiaries of his reported in-house productivity gains. CISOs, administrators, operations teams and lead lawyers must govern access and records. Software providers can supply compatible servers and apps. The interviewees do not quantify job losses, staffing changes, client fees, market shares or access-to-justice effects; Harvey is discussed as an AI client/vendor, not an ALSP.
